title: Now, Discover Your Strengths
authors: Marcus Buckingham and Donald O. Clifton

facts.claim: The book's authors are Marcus Buckingham and Donald O. Clifton (Gallup), published 2001.
The question: 'At work, do you have the opportunity to do what you do best every day?'
facts.source: Gallup Business Journal (Jan 2001 book excerpt); book text

facts.claim: Globally, only 20 percent of employees working in the large organizations Gallup surveyed feel their strengths are in play every day. The wider database behind the question: more than 1.7 million employees in 101 companies in 63 countries. The 20 percent is the share who strongly agree.
facts.source: Gallup Business Journal; book text; Fast Company

facts.claim: Gallup meta-analysis: 198,000 employees, 7,939 business units, 36 companies. Employees who strongly agreed were 50 percent more likely to work in business units with lower turnover, 38 percent more likely in more productive units, 44 percent more likely in units with higher customer satisfaction scores. These are associations, not proven causation.
Business units that increased their number of strongly agreeing employees saw matching gains in productivity, customer loyalty and retention.
Two assumptions most organizations are built on: each person can learn to be competent in almost anything; each person's greatest room for growth is in the areas of greatest weakness.
The best managers assume instead: each person's talents are enduring and unique; each person's greatest room for growth is in the areas of greatest strength.

Gallup's study of excellence involved a little over two million interviews, with groups such as best teachers, doctors, salespeople, lawyers, professional basketball players, stockbrokers, accountants, hotel housekeepers, leaders, soldiers, nurses, pastors, systems engineers and chief executives.
Before that, Gallup interviewed 80,000 managers over thirty years (the research behind First, Break All the Rules).
The authors argue that parents, teachers, managers and psychology's focus on pathology push us to become experts in our weaknesses while strengths stay dormant and neglected.
Talent: 'any recurring pattern of thought, feeling, or behavior that can be productively applied.'
Weakness: 'anything that gets in the way of excellent performance.'
Strength: the ability is a strength only if you can fathom yourself doing it repeatedly, happily and successfully (consistent near-perfect performance is the goal).

Clues to talent in the book: yearnings ('particularly when felt early in life'), rapid learning, satisfactions ('the last clue'). Under satisfactions the book suggests seeing whether you become absorbed in an activity to such an extent that you lose track of time. Spontaneous reactions are also listed among the clues in secondary sources.
facts.source: book quotes via Goodreads; Gallup clue lists

facts.claim: The StrengthsFinder profile reports a person's five most powerful signature themes out of 34 themes; Gallup built profiles from more than two million people over about 25 years.

Gallup's four warning signs of an organization on wrong assumptions, remedial fixes as damage control, and what the best managers do (talent in every role, outcomes, treat people differently, most time with best people).
facts.source: Gallup Business Journal, January 2001 book excerpt

facts.claim: The longer an employee stays and the higher they climb, the less likely they are to strongly agree that they play to their strengths; 'eight out of ten feel somewhat miscast' (source of that figure unclear); 40 percent used as example of doubling and 60 percent called not too aggressive for great organizations.
Knowledge consists of the facts and lessons learned; skills are the steps of an activity; a skill is designed to make the secrets of the best easily transferable.
'There is one sure way to identify your greatest potential for strength: step back and watch yourself for a while.'
'While your spontaneous reactions provide the clearest trace of your talents, here are three more clues': yearnings, rapid learning, satisfactions.
'When we studied them, excellent performers were rarely well rounded. On the contrary, they were sharp.' Avoiding strengths to focus on weaknesses 'isn't a sign of diligent humility.'
Since talents are enduring, spend a great deal of time and money selecting people properly; the authors do not say you should always forgo weakness fixing, but the focus belongs on strengths.
